issues.item: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' directly conflicts with 'Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts' within the same maladaptive strategies node. Excessive work engagement and avoidance of work/study are opposing coping patterns and, without any qualifier distinguishing contexts, are clinically contradictory.

vignette: Samantha, a 19-year-old fisherman from Oceania, has been haunted by the traumatic event she witnessed while out on her fishing boat. It was a harrowing experience when she saw another crew member fall overboard and drown, leaving Samantha feeling overwhelmed with guilt for not being able to save him. Since that day, Samantha has found herself reacting intensely to various triggers. The sound of footsteps behind her or nearby can send shivers down her spine, as if danger is always lurking. Even related sounds like the creaking of a bicycle chain remind her of the incident, evoking an intense fear and anxiety. These triggers are so powerful because they transport her back to that moment when she felt utterly helpless. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, Samantha has turned to overworking herself on the fishing boat, avoiding any moments where she might be alone with her thoughts. She also spends long hours on her phone or playing games as a way to escape from reality and avoid thinking about what happened. The more she engages in these maladaptive strategies, the less control she feels she has over her emotions and reactions. Samantha’s body reacts instinctively to perceived danger before she can even process what is happening. This fight-or-flight response is relentless, even when there is no real threat present. She often struggles with concentration at work because her mind keeps wandering back to that traumatic event, making it difficult for her to focus on her tasks. One of the most distressing aspects of Samantha’s experience is how the memory of the incident intrudes into her thoughts without any clear visual recollection. It’s as if she feels the full emotional intensity of the event but cannot conjure a specific image to go with it. This uncontrolled access to the memory further exacerbates her feelings of guilt and fear, making her believe that she will not be able to control her anger and do something terrible in the future. The sense that she failed to protect others has become a recurring theme in Samantha’s life. She feels as though her body is still reacting as if she were still in danger, even when she knows logically that she is safe. This constant state of hypervigilance has taken a toll on her relationships and work performance. Samantha had come to believe that the guilt she felt was a direct result of her failure to prevent the accident. This belief often manifests as intrusive memories, which in turn leads her to overwork herself or escape into screens, further intensifying her negative appraisals and fear responses. As these cycles continue, Samantha feels increasingly trapped by her own thoughts and reactions. The more she engages in maladaptive strategies like overworking and screen escapism, the stronger her memory intrusions become. This not only heightens her sense of threat but also reinforces her belief that she is unable to control her anger or protect others. The constant loop of fear, guilt, and avoidance has made it challenging for Samantha to function normally in her daily life. What finally brought Samantha to seek help was a recent incident where the sound of footsteps behind her caused her to panic so severely that she almost crashed her bicycle on the way home from work. This event was a wake-up call, as she realized that her maladaptive strategies were no longer sustainable and could lead to serious consequences. Samantha is most afraid of losing control completely and doing something terrible in response to her overwhelming emotions. At the same time, she hopes for a future where she can feel safe and regain some sense of normalcy in her life without being constantly haunted by the memory of that traumatic event.
